docs.title: Running on HPC
docs.text:
Everything needed to run on a cluster is in the HPC/ folder of the repository:

File Purpose HPC/SBO_apptainer.def Apptainer definition: Python 3.10 and the locked runtime dependencies. HPC/build_apptainer.sh Builds HPC/SBO_apptainer.sif against the cluster's OpenMPI module. HPC/example_SLURM_job.sbatch Minimal SLURM job that runs a script with MPI in the image.

The module names in the build script (2024r1, openmpi/4.1.6) are those of the cluster used for the thesis; adapt them to yours.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
The image does not contain the source code: bind-mount the repository at /app (PYTHONPATH inside the container points to /app/src), so code changes take effect without rebuilding the image. The image also expects the host MPI at the paths it was built against:

Container path Host path /app The repository root. /host-mpi-root The OpenMPI installation the image was built against. /host-dep-lib A directory with the non-system libraries libmpi.so needs.

Launch with the host MPI, which starts one container per rank:

module load openmpi                 # adapt to your cluster
MPI_ROOT=$(ompi_info --path prefix -l 0 | awk '{print $NF}')

mpirun -n 4 apptainer exec \
    --bind "$PWD":/app \
    --bind "$MPI_ROOT":/host-mpi-root \
    --bind /path/to/dep-libs:/host-dep-lib \
    HPC/SBO_apptainer.sif \
    python /app/examples/04_multi_point_optimisation.py

The container limits BLAS/OpenMP threads to one per process (OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 etc.), so the parallelism comes from the MPI ranks only. See Multi-point Optimisation for how the ranks are used.

docs.title: The Dependency Library Directory
docs.text:
build_apptainer.sh copies the libraries that libmpi.so needs (except system libraries such as libc) into a temporary directory, which it deletes after the build. Recreate it for your jobs in the same way:

MPI_LIB=$(ompi_info --path libdir -l 0 | awk '{print $NF}')
DEP_LIBS=$HOME/sbo-dep-libs
mkdir -p "$DEP_LIBS"
ldd "$MPI_LIB/libmpi.so" | awk '{print $3}' | grep '^/' \
    | grep -vE 'libc\.so|libm\.so|libpthread\.so|libdl\.so|librt\.so|libutil\.so|libresolv\.so|libgcc_s\.so' \
    | grep -v "$MPI_LIB" | xargs -r cp -t "$DEP_LIBS"

docs.title: Job Script
docs.text:
HPC/example_SLURM_job.sbatch is a minimal job script. It stages the dependency libraries for the job, and then runs a Python script on all ranks with the host MPI:

#!/bin/bash
# Minimal SLURM job: runs a Python script with MPI in the SBO Apptainer image.
# Submit from the repository root:  sbatch HPC/example_SLURM_job.sbatch [script]
# The script defaults to the multi-point example. Adapt the #SBATCH lines and the module name to your cluster.
#SBATCH --job-name=sbo
#SBATCH --ntasks=4                  # number of MPI ranks
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=2G
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
##SBATCH --partition=<partition>   # uncomment if your cluster needs these
##SBATCH --account=<account>

set -e

SCRIPT=${1:-examples/04_multi_point_optimisation.py}   # path relative to the repository root

module load openmpi                 # the OpenMPI module the image was built against (see build_apptainer.sh)
MPI_ROOT=$(ompi_info --path prefix -l 0 | awk '{print $NF}')
MPI_LIB=$(ompi_info --path libdir -l 0 | awk '{print $NF}')

# The non-system libraries libmpi.so needs, mounted at /host-dep-lib (as in build_apptainer.sh). The directory is in
# the repository, so it is reachable from every node of a multi-node job.
DEP_LIBS="$PWD/.dep-libs-$SLURM_JOB_ID"
mkdir -p "$DEP_LIBS"
trap 'rm -rf "$DEP_LIBS"' EXIT
ldd "$MPI_LIB/libmpi.so" | awk '{print $3}' | grep '^/' \
    | grep -vE 'libc\.so|libm\.so|libpthread\.so|libdl\.so|librt\.so|libutil\.so|libresolv\.so|libgcc_s\.so' \
    | grep -v "$MPI_LIB" | xargs -r cp -t "$DEP_LIBS"

# One container per rank; the repository is mounted at /app, and logs/ is written there
mpirun -n "$SLURM_NTASKS" apptainer exec \
    --bind "$PWD":/app \
    --bind "$MPI_ROOT":/host-mpi-root \
    --bind "$DEP_LIBS":/host-dep-lib \
    --pwd /app \
    HPC/SBO_apptainer.sif \
    python "/app/$SCRIPT"

Adapt the #SBATCH resources (and the partition and account, if your cluster needs them) and the OpenMPI module name. Submit it from the repository root, optionally with the script to run:

sbatch HPC/example_SLURM_job.sbatch                               # runs examples/04_multi_point_optimisation.py
sbatch HPC/example_SLURM_job.sbatch examples/05_run_from_config/05_run_from_config.py

The log files are written per rank to logs/ in the repository (see Logging).

docs.title: Building the Image
docs.text:
From the repository root on a login node:

nohup ./HPC/build_apptainer.sh > build.log 2>&1 &
tail -f build.log                # follow the build

The image is written to HPC/SBO_apptainer.sif. Rebuild it whenever uv.lock changes.

docs.title: How the Image Is Built
docs.text:
The image installs exactly the runtime dependencies pinned in uv.lock, plus the benchmarks extra (mf2), without test, docs or development tools, so it matches the environment of the thesis runs.

mpi4py is the exception: it is built from source inside the container against the host's OpenMPI, so MPI communication goes through the cluster's own (interconnect-aware) MPI library. build_apptainer.sh therefore:

  1. loads the cluster's OpenMPI module;
  2. binds the OpenMPI installation into the build at /host-mpi-root, and the non-system libraries libmpi.so depends on at /host-dep-lib;
  3. runs apptainer build from the repository root, so the definition file can copy in pyproject.toml and uv.lock.

Licence of the image

The built image contains GPL-licensed software (mf2 and the Linux base system). The definition file itself is part of this MIT-licensed repository; if you publish a built image, the GPL terms apply to it.

docs.title: Multi-fidelity Optimisation
docs.text: In a multi-fidelity optimisation, cheaper approximations of the objective (lower fidelities, e.g. a coarse mesh or a simpler model) are combined with the expensive high-fidelity (HF) function. A multi-fidelity surrogate learns from all of them, and the infill strategy decides per new point which fidelity is worth evaluating, so fewer expensive HF calls are needed.

docs.title: Setting It Up
docs.text:
1. Pass the functions ordered from high to low fidelity: functions=[f_hf, f_lf1, f_lf2]. Fidelity level 0 is the HF function.
  2. Choose a multi-fidelity surrogate and an infill strategy that chooses the fidelity:
Surrogate Infill strategies Notes HK (hierarchical Kriging) TwoStep, Random, EI/GEI (HF only) Verified. Each fidelity level needs at least 2 samples. MFK (SMT multi-fidelity Kriging) EI/GEI (HF only), Random Not verified. Needs nested samples (nested is switched on). Does not provide variance per fidelity, so not TwoStep.

TwoStep works in two steps: a single-fidelity infill strategy (single_fid_infill, default EI) chooses the location on the HF surrogate, and then the cheapest fidelity whose prediction at that location is close enough to the HF prediction (Jensen-Shannon distance below jsd_threshold, default 0.7) is evaluated. EI and GEI only sample the HF function in a multi-fidelity run.

With a single function, HK is replaced by KRG (see Defining a Problem).

docs.title: Initial Samples
docs.text: With the default settings, the number_initial_samples Latin hypercube points are spread over the fidelity levels at random, and every level is topped up to at least two samples. With "nested": True, NestedLHS is used instead: every lower-fidelity level contains the points of the higher levels, which some models (such as MFK) need.

docs.title: Emulating Expensive Functions
docs.text:
To test how a strategy behaves when the fidelities have different costs, function_delay adds an artificial delay per fidelity, in seconds, ordered from HF to LF:

settings = {"function_delay": [10.0, 1.0]}   # HF takes 10 s, LF 1 s

If the list is shorter than the number of fidelities, the last value is used for the remaining levels (with a warning). The final evaluation of the surrogate optimum is never delayed.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
examples/03_multi_fidelity_optimisation.py minimises x² with two lower-fidelity versions, using HK and TwoStep:

"""
Basic multi-fidelity optimisation.

The minimal setup to perform a multi-fidelity optimisation.

Expected output:
    Optimum at x = [0], f = 0.

Run with:
    python examples/03_multi_fidelity_optimisation.py
"""

import numpy as np

from sbo import SBO, Config


# Define the objective functions
def optimisation_function_hf(x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """The optimisation function."""
    return x**2


def optimisation_function_lf1(x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """The first low-fidelity function."""
    return x**2 + 1


def optimisation_function_lf2(x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """The second low-fidelity function."""
    return x**2 + 2


# Set the list of functions. The functions should be ordered from HF -> LF
functions = [
    optimisation_function_hf,
    optimisation_function_lf1,
    optimisation_function_lf2,
]

# Generate the config file to define the optimisation problem
config = Config(
    used_algorithms={
        "optimisation": "EgoSequential",
        "infill": "TwoStep",
        "surrogate": "HK",
    },
    lb=[-5],
    ub=[5],
    functions=functions,
)

# Instantiate the sbo
sbo = SBO(config)

# Run the optimisation
# The optimum has the type dict: {'coord': np.ndarray, 'value': float, 'fid': int}
optimum = sbo.run()

docs.title: Multi-point Optimisation
docs.text:
When one function evaluation takes long, evaluating several points at the same time shortens the wall-clock time. The multi-point optimisers use MPI: every MPI rank is a process that can evaluate the objective function.

MPI required

EgoMPI and EgoAsync need an MPI implementation (OpenMPI, MPICH or MS-MPI), mpi4py, and at least two ranks. Otherwise they fall back to EgoSequential with a warning in the log.

docs.title: Synchronous or Asynchronous
docs.text: EgoMPI (synchronous) EgoAsync (asynchronous) Points per round number_new_points per iteration, at most one per rank One new point for every rank that becomes free Who evaluates All ranks, including rank 0 Ranks 1 to N-1; rank 0 only runs the optimiser Waits for All points of the iteration Nothing: a free rank gets a new point immediately Iterations Yes (max_iterations applies) No (results are numbered in arrival order; max_iterations is not used) Best when Evaluation times are similar Evaluation times differ (e.g. multi-fidelity)

docs.title: How Several Points Are Chosen
docs.text:
An infill strategy proposes one point from the current surrogate. To propose more points before the results are known, the optimiser temporarily adds the pending points to the surrogate with an assumed value, and asks the infill strategy again. The assumed value is set by multipoint_algorithm (under "optimisation"):

  • "KB" (Kriging Believer, default): the surrogate's own prediction at the pending point, at the point's fidelity when the surrogate supports that (HK, MFK), and the HF prediction otherwise.
  • "CL" (Constant Liar): one constant value for all pending points, the minimum, mean or maximum (constant_liar_lie) of the sample values of the highest fidelity that has samples.

Proposed points that duplicate a sample, a pending point, or another point of the same batch are replaced by the same location at a higher fidelity, or by a random point if no higher fidelity is available.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
Start the script with the MPI launcher, with one process per rank. Every rank runs the same script:

mpiexec -n 4 python examples/04_multi_point_optimisation.py

sbo.run() must be called on every rank. Only rank 0 returns the optimum; the other ranks return an empty dict, so save or print the results on rank 0 only:

from mpi4py import MPI

optimum = sbo.run()
if MPI.COMM_WORLD.Get_rank() == 0:
    print(optimum)

On a cluster, see Running on HPC.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
examples/04_multi_point_optimisation.py minimises x² with EgoAsync:

"""
Basic multi-point optimisation.

The minimal setup to perform a multi-point optimisation.
Note that for running multi-point optimisations MPI should be installed. And at least
two ranks should be available. Otherwise the optimisation will be run using a
single-point optimisation (EgoSequential)

Expected output:
    Optimum at x = [0], f = 0.

Run with:
    mpiexec -n <N_CORES> python examples/04_multi_point_optimisation.py
With:
    - The mpiexec call can depend per used MPI.
    - <N_CORES> should be replaced with the number of cores to be used.
"""

import numpy as np

from sbo import SBO, Config


# Define the objective function
def optimisation_function(x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """The optimisation function."""
    return x**2


# Generate the config file to define the optimisation problem
config = Config(
    used_algorithms={
        "optimisation": "EgoAsync",
        "infill": "EI",
        "surrogate": "KRG",
    },
    lb=[-5],
    ub=[5],
    functions=[optimisation_function],
)

# Instantiate the sbo
sbo = SBO(config)

# Run the optimisation
# The optimum has the type dict: {'coord': np.ndarray, 'value': float, 'fid': int}
# Note: only rank 0 returns the optimum, all other ranks return an empty dict.
# The sbo.run() should be called on every rank.
optimum = sbo.run()

docs.title: The Optimum
docs.text:
sbo.run() (or sbo(), or the sbo.optimum property) returns the best point found:

Key Meaning coord Location of the optimum, np.ndarray of shape (n_dimensions,). value High-fidelity objective value at coord. fid Fidelity level; always 0 (high fidelity) for the optimum. start_time, end_time Wall-clock times (time.time()) of the evaluation, if the point was evaluated by the optimiser. mpi_rank The MPI rank that evaluated the point.

The optimum is the best of the high-fidelity samples and of the optimum of the final surrogate, which is evaluated once more on the high-fidelity function at the end of the run. In multi-point runs only rank 0 returns it; the other ranks return {}.

docs.title: Optimisation Data
docs.text:
sbo.optimisation_data holds the data of the whole run, as a dict with one entry per iteration plus a few summary entries:

Key Contents "config" The problem: bounds, function names, number of fidelities and dimensions, settings and used algorithms. "init" The initial samples (sample_points) before the first iteration. 0, 1, 2, ... One entry per iteration (see below). For EgoAsync: "000000", "000001", ... per received result, in arrival order. "final" EgoAsync only: the state after all workers stopped. "total" The latest values, the total function_calls and the total time_elapsed of the run. "solution" The optimum (the same dict as returned by run()).

Each iteration entry contains:

Key Contents best_value, best_coord Best high-fidelity sample so far. surrogate_optimum Optimum of the surrogate (coord, value), used by the convergence criteria. infill_value Infill value of the selected point(s), e.g. the expected improvement. function_calls, function_calls_HF Number of calls so far, per fidelity ({fid: count}) and for the HF function. sample_points All samples so far, per fidelity ({fid: [points]}). time_elapsed Duration of the iteration in seconds. time_since_start EgoAsync only: seconds since the start of the run.

For example, the convergence history:

data = sbo.optimisation_data
iterations = [k for k in data if isinstance(k, int)]
history = [data[k]["best_value"] for k in iterations]

docs.title: Saving and Loading
docs.text:
save_optimisation_data writes the optimisation data as a pickle file to the save_folder setting (default "results", created if needed):

sbo.save_optimisation_data("my_run")     # -> results/my_run.pkl

Load it again with pickle:

import pickle

with open("results/my_run.pkl", "rb") as f:
    data = pickle.load(f)

docs.title: Plotting
docs.text:
For 1D and 2D problems, plot_surrogate draws the surrogate, the samples and the next sample location for each iteration, one subplot per iteration:

sbo.plot_surrogate(
    "My run",
    filename="my_run.png",          # relative paths are saved in save_folder; None: don't save
    show=False,                     # True: open a window
    up_to=5,                        # only iterations before 5 (optional)
    iterations=[0, 2, 4],           # or exactly these iterations (optional)
    true_functions_plot=[0],        # also draw the true function(s) of these fidelities (1D only)
    fid_samples_plot=[0, 1],        # only show samples of these fidelities (default: all)
)

In 1D the plot also shows the 95% confidence band of the surrogate (if it has a variance) and the infill function on a second axis. Plotting temporarily re-trains the surrogate on the samples of each iteration and restores it afterwards. For problems with more than two dimensions, plot_surrogate only logs a warning.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
By default, Config uses the logger default_logger, which writes to logs/default_logger_<timestamp>.log in the working directory (one file per rank in MPI runs) and also prints warnings and errors to the screen.

To log somewhere else, pass your own logger. setup_logger creates one:

import logging
from sbo.utils.Logger import setup_logger

logger = setup_logger("my_run", level=logging.INFO, to_file=False)   # print to stdout
config = Config(..., logger=logger)
setup_logger argument Default Meaning name "default_logger" Name of the logger and of the log file. level logging.INFO Lowest level that is logged. save_dir "logs" Folder for the log file. to_file True Write to a file (True) or to stdout (False). overwrite False Overwrite an existing log file instead of appending.

At logging.DEBUG level every call of the objective function and its result are logged as well.

Warnings worth checking in the log: ignored or replaced settings, algorithms that were replaced (e.g. HK → KRG, EgoAsync → EgoSequential), and a short function_delay list.

docs.title: Settings and Stopping Criteria
docs.text: Every algorithm has default settings, so settings only needs the values you want to change. The Settings Reference lists every setting with its description, type, default and allowed values.

docs.title: Passing Settings
docs.text:
General settings go at the top level; settings for the selected algorithms go in a nested dict under "surrogate", "infill" or "optimisation":

settings = {
    "random_seed": 0,                              # general setting
    "number_initial_samples": 10,
    "infill": {"g": 5},                            # setting of the selected infill strategy (GEI)
    "optimisation": {"max_function_calls": 50},    # setting of the selected optimisation algorithm
}
config = Config(..., settings=settings)

Only the settings of the selected algorithms are available: with "infill": "EI", the GEI setting g is unknown.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
examples/02_custom_settings.py runs GEI with g = 5, a budget of 50 function calls and a fixed seed:

"""
Single fidelity optimisation with custom settings.

The settings passed to the optimiser can be changed by the config instance.
The available settings depend on the used algorithms; all of them are listed in the
Settings Reference of the documentation.

Expected output:
    Optimum at x = [0], f = 0.

Run with:
    python examples/02_custom_settings.py
"""

import numpy as np

from sbo import SBO, Config


# Define the objective function
def optimisation_function(x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """The optimisation function."""
    return x**2


# Set the custom settings
settings = {
    "infill": {"g": 5},
    "optimisation": {"max_function_calls": 50},
    "random_seed": 0,
}

# Generate the config file to define the optimisation problem
config = Config(
    used_algorithms={
        "optimisation": "EgoSequential",
        "infill": "GEI",
        "surrogate": "KRG",
    },
    lb=[-5],
    ub=[5],
    functions=[optimisation_function],
    settings=settings,
)

# Instantiate the sbo
sbo = SBO(config)

# Run the optimisation
# The optimum has the type dict: {'coord': np.ndarray, 'value': float, 'fid': int}
optimum = sbo.run()

docs.title: Reading Settings
docs.text:
config.get("random_seed")                   # general setting
config.get("optimisation.max_iterations")   # nested setting, dot notation
config["infill"]["g"]                        # dict access also works

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
All settings are checked when Config is created:

  • an unknown key is ignored;
  • a value of the wrong type is replaced by the default (an int is accepted, and converted, where a float is expected; a JSON list is converted to a tuple where a tuple is expected);
  • a value below the minimum or above the maximum is replaced by that minimum or maximum;
  • a value that is not one of the allowed values is replaced by the default.

By default each of these only logs a warning, which the default logger also prints to the screen. To get an error instead, set "strict_validation": True:

config = Config(..., settings={"strict_validation": True, "number_initial_samples": 1})
# ValueError: Value for setting 'number_initial_samples' (1) is below the minimum of 2 ...

docs.title: Commonly Used Settings
docs.text: Setting Default Description random_seed 42 Seed for the initial samples, the internal optimisers and all random choices. number_initial_samples 5 Number of initial samples if none are passed to SBO (at least 2). number_new_points 2 Points proposed per iteration in a multi-point run; see Multi-point. nested False Nested initial samples for multi-fidelity: every lower-fidelity level also has the higher-fidelity points. function_delay None Artificial delay per fidelity in seconds, e.g. to emulate expensive functions in tests. save_folder "results" Folder for save_optimisation_data and plots; see Results. strict_validation False Raise a ValueError for invalid settings instead of warning. infill_opt_*, surrogate_opt_* Settings of the differential evolution that optimises the infill function and finds the surrogate optimum.

docs.title: Stopping Criteria
docs.text:
The optimisation stops as soon as any criterion is met. Each one is a setting under "optimisation"; set it to None to switch it off.

Setting Default Stops when max_iterations 300 max_iterations iterations are completed. Not used by EgoAsync, which has no iterations. max_function_calls 1000 The total number of function calls (all fidelities) reaches the budget. max_function_calls_HF 150 The number of high-fidelity calls reaches the budget. convergence_threshold 1e-6 The surrogate optimum changed by less than this over the last convergence_window iterations. relative_convergence_threshold 1e-6 The same, relative to the earlier surrogate optimum. convergence_window 5 Number of iterations used by the two convergence criteria. min_infill_value 1e-6 The infill value (e.g. the expected improvement) of the new point drops below this.

Function-call budgets include the final evaluation

After the loop, the optimum of the surrogate is evaluated once more on the high-fidelity function. The function-call budgets reserve one HF call for this, so max_function_calls_HF = 50 gives at most 50 HF calls in total.

The convergence criteria compare the surrogate optimum (the minimum of the high-fidelity surrogate), not the best sample found: the surrogate optimum also changes when new samples change the model.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
random_seed seeds the initial samples, the differential evolution of the infill and surrogate optimisation, the surrogate models (their own seed setting is set to random_seed), and config.rng, which is used for every other random choice. Two runs with the same problem, settings and seed therefore give the same result.

The thesis results were produced with the locked environment (uv sync --locked --no-dev --extra benchmarks); other package versions can give slightly different numbers.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Most problems are reported in the log; see Logging for where it is.

docs.title: My Multi-point Run Is Sequential
docs.text:
The log says that EgoMPI or EgoAsync continues with EgoSequential. Check that:

  • an MPI implementation and mpi4py are installed (python -c "from mpi4py import MPI; print(MPI.Get_version())");
  • the script is started with the MPI launcher and at least two ranks: mpiexec -n 4 python script.py;
  • on a cluster, the container is started once per rank by the host MPI (see Running on HPC).

docs.title: A Setting Has No Effect
docs.text:
Settings with an unknown key, a wrong type or an invalid value are ignored or replaced, with a warning (see Validation). Common causes:

  • the setting belongs to another algorithm than the selected one (e.g. g without "infill": "GEI");
  • an algorithm setting is at the top level instead of under "surrogate", "infill" or "optimisation".

Set "strict_validation": True to get an error instead of a warning.

docs.title: The Optimisation Stops Too Early or Too Late
docs.text: Check which stopping criterion was met (logged at INFO level) and the Stopping Criteria. The convergence criteria with their defaults of 1e-6 can stop a run early on a flat function; set them to None to run until the budget is used.

docs.title: The Algorithm Is Not the One I Selected
docs.text: HK with one function becomes KRG, FilteredGEI with one function becomes GEI, and EgoMPI/EgoAsync without MPI become EgoSequential; see Algorithms. sbo.config.used_algorithms shows the algorithms in use.

docs.title: A Second Problem Uses the First Problem's Settings
docs.text: Config is a singleton: a second Config(...) re-initialises the same instance, and every existing SBO sees the new problem. Create a new SBO after the new Config, or call Config.destroy_instance() first; see Config Is a Singleton.

docs.title: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mf2'
docs.text: Config.from_json and example 05 use the mf2 benchmark functions, an optional dependency. Install them with pip install "multi-fidelity-multi-point-sbo[benchmarks]" (or uv sync --extra benchmarks).

docs.title: ValueError: Not all ub > lb.
docs.text: Every upper bound must be strictly larger than its lower bound, and lb and ub must have the same length. To move both bounds of an existing config, use config.set_bounds(lb, ub).

docs.title: NotImplementedError When Creating the Optimiser
docs.text: CEI and CoKRG are not implemented yet, and FilteredGEI needs CoKRG for more than one fidelity. See the status of every algorithm on the home page.
